> **The research decision.** Decide which studies count before you see a single
> result, how you will find every one of them, and whether combining them answers
> your question or only averages their biases. A tool can search, sort, and pool
> in seconds, but only you can defend why each study is in the pile and what the
> pooled number is allowed to mean.

## Why this decision matters

**The decision on the table: whether your pile of studies is a fair sample of the
evidence, and whether one number can honestly speak for it.**

> *"Tell me how a study got into your review before you tell me what the studies
> found. If you picked them after reading their results, your average is an
> opinion with a confidence interval attached."*
> — a **review-journal methods editor**, reading a manuscript that pooled twenty
> canvassing experiments into one estimate of persuasion

Once your question has been studied more than a few times, the most useful thing
you can contribute may be a careful account of what those studies, taken together,
actually say. That work has a trap built into it. A review can look exhaustive and
still be a biased sample, because the studies that reach print are often the ones
that found something. Pool a biased sample and you get a biased answer with a
narrow interval, which is worse than no answer, because it looks settled. This
chapter gives you the decisions that make a synthesis worth trusting, and the
habit of saying exactly how far its number reaches.

## The concept

Evidence synthesis sits in the complex-designs chapter of the design library in
RDSS, which declares a meta-analysis as a design in its own right: the inquiry is
the average of the true effects across studies and how much those true effects
vary, and the answer strategy is a weighted average of the study estimates
[@blair2023rdss]. That framing matters because it makes a review a research design
with its own data strategy, not a reading list.

**Evidence synthesis** is the family of methods that answers a question by
collecting, appraising, and combining the studies that already exist on it.
Example: gathering every randomized experiment on door-to-door canvassing to ask
how much a single conversation moves support for a candidate. It comes in two main
shapes. A **scoping review** is a synthesis that maps what has been studied, how,
where, and with which gaps, without pooling results into one number
[@arksey2005scoping]. Example: charting which countries, election types, and
outcome measures the canvassing literature covers. A **systematic review** is a
synthesis that answers a focused question with a prespecified search, explicit
eligibility rules, an appraisal of each study, and often a pooled estimate
[@higgins2024cochrane]. Example: estimating the average effect of canvassing on
turnout among randomized experiments published or posted before a fixed date.

Everything starts from a **protocol**, a written plan that fixes the question, the
eligibility rules, the search, and the analysis before you screen anything.
Example: a one-page document saying "randomized field experiments, any country,
outcome is candidate support or turnout, searched in three named databases on a
named date." Researchers often frame the question with **PICO** (population,
intervention, comparison, outcome) for effect questions, or **PCC** (population,
concept, context) for scoping questions. Example: registered voters in general
elections (population), a face-to-face canvassing visit (intervention), no visit
(comparison), stated support for the candidate (outcome). Posting the protocol on a public registry
such as the Open Science Framework before you start gives it a date stamp. The
point is the same one that governs any design: decide what counts before the
results can tempt you.

The data strategy of a review has four recorded steps. A **search log** is the
exact record of where you searched, with which strings, on which dates, and how
many records came back. Example: "Database X, 12 March, string `canvass* AND
(persua* OR vote choice) AND experiment*`, 412 records." Anyone should be able to
rerun it. **Screening** is the two-stage filter that applies eligibility rules you
wrote down before searching. Example: at the first stage you read titles and
abstracts and send anything unclear forward; at the second you read full texts and
give every study you exclude one reason from a list fixed in advance, such as "not
randomized" or "no usable estimate." The standard is two people screening every
record without seeing each other's calls. When that is out of reach, a second
person screens at least a random share at each stage, and the agreement and how
you settled each disagreement go in the log [@higgins2024cochrane]. An AI tool can propose first-pass calls,
but it is an assistant, not your independent second screener, and it never
excludes a record nobody has read. Independence means two judgments made without
seeing each other, and a person who reads the tool's call before deciding tends to
agree with it. The same split runs through the whole route.
AI tools are fast at drafting search strings, removing duplicate records, proposing
first-pass screening calls, and filling a draft extraction row. They are also known
to invent studies that do not exist, to name databases as they were years ago, and
to copy the wrong statistic from a crowded table [@ji2023hallucination]. Every one
of those outputs is a lead until you have opened the source yourself.

The **PRISMA flow diagram** is the standard chart of how many records you found, removed, screened, and kept, with the reason
for every study excluded at full text [@page2021prisma]. It reports what you did.
Its authors say plainly that PRISMA is a reporting guideline, not a tool for
judging a review's quality, so a tidy diagram certifies nothing about the studies
inside it. Scoping reviews have their own reporting
extension [@tricco2018prismascr]. An **extraction form** is the fixed table you fill
for every study: design, sample, setting, estimate, its uncertainty, and anything
that threatens it. Example: one row per canvassing experiment, with the effect in
percentage points and its standard error (how far the estimate would typically
move if the study were run again on a new sample) copied from the study's results table.

The form holds one row per study, and that rule needs defending. **Dependent
results** are several estimates that come from the same study's participants, so
they rise and fall together. Example: one canvassing experiment that reports
effects on candidate support and on turnout, at two survey waves, for two scripts
compared against one shared control group. Entering those as separate studies
counts the same households several times and makes the pooled interval narrower
than the evidence. Write a rule in your protocol, before you extract, for choosing
one estimate per study (for instance, the outcome the authors named as primary, at
the longest follow-up), or combine the estimates within the study, or use a method
built for dependent results [@higgins2024cochrane; @borenstein2021introduction].

Two appraisal steps come next. **Risk of bias** is your study-by-study judgment of
whether the design and conduct could have tilted the result. Example: an
experiment that lost a third of its households before the follow-up survey gets
flagged. Rating the **certainty of the evidence** is the final judgment of how much
trust the whole body deserves, weighing risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness
(studies that answer a slightly different question from yours), imprecision, and
missing studies [@higgins2024cochrane]. Example: six well-run experiments that agree
earn more trust than twenty small ones that scatter.

Then, if pooling is defensible, the answer strategy. An **effect size** is each
study's result expressed on one shared scale, so studies can be compared. Example:
every canvassing effect converted to percentage points of support. A
**meta-analysis** is the statistical combination of those effect sizes into one
weighted average with an interval [@borenstein2021introduction]. The weights come
from **inverse-variance weighting**, which means each study counts in proportion to
its precision. Example: a study of 20,000 households with a standard error of 0.45
points counts about ten times as much as one with a standard error of 1.4 points.
Two models set what the average means. A **fixed-effect model** assumes every study
estimates one identical true effect and differs only by chance. Example: six
replications of the same script, in the same kind of district, in the same kind of
election. A **random-effects model** assumes each setting has its own true effect
and estimates their average and their spread. Example: canvassing in different
countries and years, where a conversation may simply matter more in some places.
**Heterogeneity** is the disagreement among studies beyond what
chance alone would produce. Example: canvassing moving votes in primaries and
ballot-measure campaigns but not in general elections [@kalla2018minimal]. A
**forest plot** is a chart that shows each study's estimate and interval on one
row, with the pooled estimate as a diamond at the bottom. Example: the left panel
of the figure later in this chapter.

One habit to drop now. **Vote counting** means tallying how many studies were
statistically significant (an estimate far enough from zero that chance alone
rarely produces it) and calling the majority the answer. It misleads because a small study
can miss a real effect, so "most studies found nothing" can describe a literature
of small studies that all point the same way [@borenstein2021introduction].

Now the compass. The kind of a synthesis question comes from its words, as for any
other question. "How much does a canvassing visit change support for the
candidate?" is causal whether your pile holds randomized experiments or
observational comparisons. The designs decide what the answer can establish. A
pooled average of randomized experiments carries their assignment license to a
causal claim. A pooled average of observational comparisons does not: the question
stays causal, that pile leaves it currently unidentified, and the claim you can
make is an association unless each study defends its own identification. Pooling
never creates a crossing license. The synthesis inherits each study's warrant, and
averaging twenty confounded comparisons gives you one confounded comparison with a
smaller interval. Reach needs care too. A pooled effect question reaches for a population:
the settings where the intervention could be used. The studies you pooled were not
sampled at random from those settings, so no sampling license carries the average
there. The random-effects average describes settings like those that were studied
and reported, and saying more requires an argument about which settings are
missing. A scoping review asks a descriptive question whose population is every
eligible study, including the ones your search did not find: what has been
studied, how, and where. Its warrant is the completeness of your search, which the search log documents and a missed
database weakens, and it makes no claim about what the true effect is. This route builds on the search habits
of [Finding and Verifying Prior
Evidence](../part2-curiosity-to-design/08-finding-and-verifying-prior-evidence.qmd),
and it is a multi-part design in the sense of [Hybrid and Complex
Designs](../part3-pathways/16-hybrid-and-complex-designs.qmd): each stage of the
review carries its own error into the final number.

## A worked example

Bring this into political science. A campaign asks you whether its volunteers
should keep knocking on doors to persuade voters in a general election. You find
six randomized canvassing experiments that meet your protocol (these six are
constructed for the example). Five of them report effects too imprecise to call
significant, and one reports a clear positive effect. A quick reader says "five of
six found nothing, so canvassing does not persuade." That is vote counting, and it
is not the evidence talking.

Pool them instead. Each study's estimate goes in with a weight set by its
precision, so the large study E, with a standard error of 0.45 points, carries the
most weight. The fixed-effect average comes out at about 0.6 of a point, with an
interval running from just below zero to about 1.25 points. The random-effects
average is almost the same, because the six studies disagree little beyond chance:
the share of their spread that exceeds chance is only 7 percent. Treat that 7
percent loosely. With six studies, the spread between settings is estimated very
poorly, and the usual random-effects interval, built on the normal curve, tends
to come out too narrow when studies are this few [@higgins2024cochrane]. The
**Hartung-Knapp-Sidik-Jonkman interval** is the random-effects interval built for
that case: it scales the uncertainty to how much the studies actually scatter and
uses a wider multiplier from the t distribution, which allows for estimating the
spread from few studies. Example: with six studies the multiplier is about 2.57
instead of 1.96. It is the interval the code below reports, and the reading it
supports is modest: the pooled evidence is consistent with a small positive
average effect, cannot distinguish it from zero, and makes an average effect above
about 1.6 points unlikely for settings like these.

Political scientists have run this synthesis for real. Kalla and Broockman pooled
40 field experiments and added nine of their own, and concluded that the best
estimate of campaign contact's persuasive effect in United States general
elections is zero, a finding that sets a sober prior for any campaign reading your
review [@kalla2018minimal].

The block below pools the six constructed studies both ways, counts the votes, and
then repeats the pool after one extraction slip. Watch what happens to the
interval when one number lands in the wrong column.

```python
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
from scipy import stats

# Six canvassing experiments, CONSTRUCTED for this example. Each row is one
# study's effect on support for the candidate (percentage points) and its
# standard error, copied from the study's own results table. One row per study:
# where a study reported several estimates, the protocol's rule picked one.
studies = pd.DataFrame({
    "study":    ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"],
    "estimate": [2.9, 0.6, -0.4, 2.4, 0.3, 1.1],
    "se":       [1.4, 0.8, 1.1, 1.7, 0.45, 0.9],
})

def pool(y, s):
    k = len(y)
    w = 1 / s**2                                   # precise studies weigh more
    fixed = np.sum(w * y) / np.sum(w)
    fixed_ci = fixed + np.array([-1.96, 1.96]) / np.sqrt(np.sum(w))
    q = np.sum(w * (y - fixed) ** 2)               # disagreement beyond chance?
    tau2 = max(0.0, (q - (k - 1)) / (np.sum(w) - np.sum(w**2) / np.sum(w)))
    wr = 1 / (s**2 + tau2)                         # weights that allow for the spread
    rand = np.sum(wr * y) / np.sum(wr)
    se_z = 1 / np.sqrt(np.sum(wr))
    z_ci = rand + np.array([-1.96, 1.96]) * se_z   # normal approximation: too narrow
    # Hartung-Knapp-Sidik-Jonkman: rescale by the scatter the studies show (never
    # below the usual standard error) and use a t multiplier on k - 1 df.
    scatter = np.sum(wr * (y - rand) ** 2) / (k - 1)
    se_h = np.sqrt(max(scatter, 1.0)) * se_z
    hk_ci = rand + np.array([-1, 1]) * stats.t.ppf(0.975, k - 1) * se_h
    # Prediction interval: where the true effect in ONE new setting may fall.
    pred = rand + np.array([-1, 1]) * stats.t.ppf(0.975, k - 2) * np.sqrt(tau2 + se_z**2)
    i2 = max(0.0, (q - (k - 1)) / q) * 100
    return dict(fixed=fixed, fixed_ci=fixed_ci, rand=rand, hk_ci=hk_ci,
                z_ci=z_ci, pred=pred, i2=i2)

def show(ci):
    return f"[{ci[0]:+.2f}, {ci[1]:+.2f}]"

y, s = studies.estimate.to_numpy(), studies.se.to_numpy()
sig = (np.abs(y / s) > 1.96).sum()
r = pool(y, s)
print(f"vote count (significant studies)  : {sig} of {len(y)}")
print(f"fixed-effect pooled estimate      : {r['fixed']:+.2f}  {show(r['fixed_ci'])}")
print(f"random-effects pooled estimate    : {r['rand']:+.2f}  {show(r['hk_ci'])}")
print(f"  same, normal-approximation CI   :        {show(r['z_ci'])}")
print(f"prediction interval, new setting  :        {show(r['pred'])}")
print(f"share of spread beyond chance (I2): {r['i2']:.0f}%")

# One extraction slip: study E's outcome STANDARD DEVIATION (48 points, from
# its descriptive table) typed into the standard-error column.
s_bad = s.copy(); s_bad[4] = 48
b = pool(y, s_bad)
print(f"\nsame pool, E's SD typed as its SE : {b['rand']:+.2f}  {show(b['hk_ci'])}")
print(f"  with the normal-approximation CI:        {show(b['z_ci'])}")
print("the largest study vanished from the average and nothing crashed")
```

The printout gives a fixed-effect estimate of +0.61 points with an interval of
-0.03 to +1.25. The random-effects estimate is +0.65, and its
Hartung-Knapp-Sidik-Jonkman interval runs from -0.27 to +1.57, wider than the -0.04
to +1.35 the normal approximation would claim. The campaign, though, is deciding
about its own next election, a setting none of the six studied. A **prediction
interval** is the range where the true effect in one new setting is likely to fall,
allowing for both the uncertainty in the average and the spread between settings.
Example: the printout's -0.56 to +1.86, which says the next election could see a
small backfire, no persuasion, or close to two points. With six studies that range is itself
rough, but it is the range the campaign's decision needs
[@higgins2024cochrane].

The last lines are the warning. With study E's standard deviation typed where its
standard error belonged, the largest study nearly disappears from the average and
the random-effects estimate jumps from +0.65 to +0.95, while the code runs without
complaint. The Hartung-Knapp-Sidik-Jonkman interval, -0.26 to +2.17, still spans
zero. Report the same pool with the normal approximation, as many default tools
do, and you get +0.03 to +1.88, which excludes it. Two routine-looking errors, one
wrong cell and one interval too narrow for six studies, together turn "cannot tell
from zero" into "persuades."

## A seeded simulation

A review can be flawless in every step you control and still inherit a bias you
cannot see: the studies that never reached print. The code below builds a world
where 30 canvassing experiments are run and the true average effect is 1.0 point.
Every study with a significant positive result gets published. Each of the others
gets out only by luck, one time in four. Then it pools the published studies the
way a careful reviewer would, and pools all 30 the way nobody can. The seed makes
the run reproduce this exact figure.

```python
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy import stats

SEED = 464
rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)

k, mu, tau = 30, 1.0, 0.5            # 30 studies RUN; true average +1.0 point
se = rng.uniform(0.3, 2.5, k)        # small studies carry large standard errors
theta = rng.normal(mu, tau, k)       # each study's own true effect
est = rng.normal(theta, se)          # what each study reports
significant = est / se > 1.96
published = significant | (rng.random(k) < 0.25)   # nulls rarely get out

def pool(y, s):                      # random-effects average, HKSJ interval
    k = len(y)
    w = 1 / s**2
    fe = np.sum(w * y) / np.sum(w)
    q = np.sum(w * (y - fe) ** 2)
    t2 = max(0.0, (q - (k - 1)) / (np.sum(w) - np.sum(w**2) / np.sum(w)))
    wr = 1 / (s**2 + t2)
    m = np.sum(wr * y) / np.sum(wr)
    scatter = np.sum(wr * (y - m) ** 2) / (k - 1)
    half = stats.t.ppf(0.975, k - 1) * np.sqrt(max(scatter, 1.0) / np.sum(wr))
    return m, m - half, m + half

all_m, all_lo, all_hi = pool(est, se)
pub_m, lo, hi = pool(est[published], se[published])
print(f"published: {published.sum()} of {k}, significant: {significant.sum()}")
print(f"pooled, all run   : {all_m:.2f} [{all_lo:.2f}, {all_hi:.2f}]")
print(f"pooled, published : {pub_m:.2f} [{lo:.2f}, {hi:.2f}]")

fig, (a1, a2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.6, 4.2))
idx = np.where(published)[0]
idx = idx[np.argsort(se[idx])]                     # most precise on top
ys = np.arange(len(idx), 0, -1) + 1.0
a1.errorbar(est[idx], ys, xerr=1.96 * se[idx], fmt="s", color="#2a78d6", ms=4)
a1.fill([lo, pub_m, hi, pub_m], [0.5, 0.85, 0.5, 0.15], color="#eb6834")
a1.axvline(0, color="#9a9a9a", lw=0.8)                 # zero effect
a1.axvline(mu, color="#333333", ls="--")               # the truth
a1.set_xlabel("Effect on support (percentage points)")
a1.set_title("What the published record shows", loc="left")
a2.scatter(est[published], se[published], color="#2a78d6", label="published")
a2.scatter(est[~published], se[~published], facecolors="none",
           edgecolors="#9a9a9a", label="never published")
grid = np.linspace(0, se.max() * 1.05, 50)
a2.plot(1.96 * grid, grid, color="#9a9a9a", ls=":", label="significance line")
a2.axvline(pub_m, color="#eb6834", label="pooled, published")
a2.axvline(all_m, color="#2a78d6", label="pooled, all run")
a2.axvline(mu, color="#333333", ls="--"); a2.invert_yaxis()
a2.set_xlabel("Effect on support (percentage points)")
a2.set_ylabel("Standard error"); a2.legend()
a2.set_title("Every study that was run", loc="left")
plt.show()
```

![Twelve published studies pool to 1.80 points, while all 30 studies that were run
pool to 1.16 against a true average of 1.0.](../images/sims/evidence_synthesis.png){fig-alt="Two-panel chart. Left: a forest plot titled what the published record shows, with 12 blue square estimates and horizontal 95 percent interval lines, one row per published study sorted by precision, a dashed black vertical line at the true average of 1.0, a grey line at zero, and an orange diamond at the bottom for the pooled published estimate, centred near 1.8 and spanning about 0.93 to 2.67, so the true average sits just inside its left tip. Right: a funnel plot titled every study that was run, with effect on the horizontal axis and standard error on an inverted vertical axis; 12 filled blue dots are published and 18 hollow grey circles were never published, all of them left of the dotted significance line; an orange vertical line marks pooled published at 1.80, a blue line marks pooled all run at 1.16, and a dashed black line marks the truth at 1.0."}

Read the left panel first, because it is all a reviewer ever sees. Twelve
published studies, most intervals overlapping, and a pooled diamond at 1.80 points
with an interval from 0.93 to 2.67. Half the rows are significant and half are
not, so a vote counter would call the literature split. The pooled estimate says
something firmer and wrong: an effect near 1.8 points, with the true average of 1.0
only just inside the lower tip of its interval.

Now the right panel, which no real reviewer can draw. It is a **funnel plot**, a
scatter of each study's estimate against its standard error, with the most precise
studies at the top. Without a publication filter the dots would spread evenly around
the true average, narrowing toward the top like an upturned funnel. Here the 18
hollow circles that never reached print all sit left of the dotted significance
line, and most of them report less than the true 1.0 point. Remove them and the
published dots lean to the right, toward large positive effects. Pool all 30 and you get 1.16 points, with an interval
from 0.72 to 1.60 that contains the truth. Pool the published 12 and the estimate
is about 55 percent larger. The size of the pile did not cause this. The filter did:
**publication bias**, the tendency of results to reach print because of what they
found.

A lopsided funnel is a warning light, not a diagnosis. Asymmetry can also come from
small studies that were run in different settings, from poor design in small
studies, or from chance, and the standard advice is to test for it only when at
least ten studies are pooled [@sterne2011recommendations; @egger1997bias]. When you see
it, you say so, you search harder for unpublished work (registries, preprints,
conference programs, emails to authors), and you report how the pooled estimate
changes when you pool only the larger, more precise studies.
In the companion notebook, change the `0.25` to `1.0` so every null is published,
rerun, and watch the two vertical lines converge.

## When one number is the wrong answer

Pooling is a choice, and often the right choice is not to make it. Four situations
call for a scoping review or a structured narrative synthesis instead.

The studies answer different questions. An economist reviewing cash-transfer
programs finds studies of unconditional grants, school-conditional grants, and
transfers paired with training. One average across them answers none of the three
questions a policymaker would ask.

The studies carry different warrants. A business analyst might hold a company's
randomized product tests beside its before-and-after comparisons of the same
features. The randomized tests have a causal license; the before-and-after
comparisons do not, and pooling them hands the weaker design the stronger design's
credibility.

The outcomes cannot share a scale. An ecologist synthesizing predator-removal
experiments may find prey counts, biomass, and survival rates. Standardized effect
sizes can put some of these on one scale, but only when you can defend that they
measure the same thing [@koricheva2013handbook; @gurevitch2018metaanalysis].

The heterogeneity is the finding. When canvassing works in primaries and not in
general elections, the average of the two is a number that describes no election.
Report the split, and treat the reason for it as the next question.

In each case the honest product is a map: a table of what was studied, in which
settings, with which designs and outcomes, and where the gaps sit. That map is a
real contribution, and it is often the one a first synthesis should aim for.

## An AI failure case

You paste the six study PDFs into an AI tool and ask it to fill your extraction form
and pool the results. It returns a clean table and a confident paragraph: "The
pooled effect is +0.95 points (95% interval +0.03 to +1.88), indicating that
canvassing reliably increases candidate support." Every row looks plausible. But
in one row the tool copied the outcome's standard deviation from a descriptive
table into the standard-error column, it built the interval on the normal
approximation that six studies cannot support, and its paragraph cites a seventh,
"confirming" study by a real-sounding author team that appears in none of your PDFs. This is two named
failures at once: **confident fabrication**, a citation and a number that no source
contains, and **silent scope change**, "cannot tell from zero" quietly upgraded to
"reliably increases." A tidy table is not an extraction. You catch it by tracing
every cell back to a page: open each PDF, find the table the number came from, and
confirm it is the standard error, not the standard deviation. Delete any citation you
cannot open. Then rerun the pool on your verified table with the
Hartung-Knapp-Sidik-Jonkman interval, write the sentence that interval licenses, and
log why the tool's version was rejected.

Commit your own answer first, then delegate. Each prompt is a checkable job, not a
request for a verdict. Work them as a loop. The first answer is a draft: find the
claim you cannot check, say so in your next message, and run it again. Some tools
will run that whole loop unattended and hand you a finished review. The finished
look is exactly what makes the questions in this chapter worth asking before you
accept it.

::: {.callout-important title="Do not delegate"}
Three calls stay yours. You decide **which studies are eligible, in writing, before
you read any result**, because a rule set after the results is a filter on the
answer. You decide **whether pooling is defensible at all**, because only you can
judge whether the studies answer one question with comparable designs and outcomes.
And you decide **what the synthesis can claim**, since it inherits every study's
warrant and no more. A tool can search, screen a first pass, and compute a weighted
average in seconds. You own the eligibility rules, the decision to pool, and the
sentence that reports it.
:::

1. Write your review question and its eligibility rules before you search. Use
   PICO for an effect question or PCC for a scoping question, and add the designs
   you accept, the date range, the languages, the reasons you will use to exclude a
   full text, and your rule for choosing one estimate when a study reports several. Then write your Research Contract
   lines for this route: the question; the estimand (the average true effect and its
   spread, or for a scoping review the map you will produce); the data strategy
   (search, screening, extraction); the answer strategy (pooling or a structured
   narrative); the warrant (the studies' own crossing licenses, never the pooling);
   and the limits (which settings and which unpublished work you may be missing).

   *When you are ready to delegate this step:*

   ```text
   Act as a systematic-review methodologist. Here is my review question and my
   eligibility rules: [paste them]. List, as a table, every term in my rules that two
   careful screeners could read differently, and for each one give an example study
   that one would include and the other would exclude. Do not rewrite my rules for me.
   ```

   *After running, verify: read each flagged ambiguity against your own question and
   tighten only the rules where the example would really split two screeners. If the
   tool finds no ambiguity at all, ask again with "assume two screeners disagree on
   10 percent of records; which rule causes it?" Counters **illusion of
   completeness**, a tidy table that implies your rules have no gaps.*
2. Build a search log you could hand to a stranger. Name each database or source,
   the exact search string, the date, and the number of records it returned, and
   add at least one route to unpublished work.

   *When you are ready to delegate this step:*

   ```text
   Act as a research librarian in political science. My review question is
   [paste it]. Suggest the databases and registries where studies on it are indexed,
   and draft one search string for each using its own syntax. Only name databases
   you are confident exist; mark anything uncertain.
   ```

   *After running, verify: run every string yourself, record the hit count and date
   in your log, and drop any database you cannot open. Counters **stale knowledge**
   (a database renamed, merged, or retired since the tool learned about it).*
3. Screen in two stages with the rules you fixed in step 1. At titles and abstracts,
   send anything unclear forward. At full texts, give every excluded study one
   reason from your list and log it. Then make a documented second check: ideally a
   second person screens every record, and at minimum a random 20 percent at each
   stage, blind to your calls, and you log the agreement and how each disagreement was settled. If no
   second person is available, say in your report that one person screened. Before
   a tool proposes calls on anything, test it on a random sample you have already
   screened blind, and never let it exclude a record you have not read.

   *When you are ready to delegate this step:*

   ```text
   Here are my eligibility rules [paste them] and 50 titles and abstracts [paste
   them]. For each record, say include, exclude, or unsure, and quote the exact words
   in the abstract that decided it. Do not decide a record from its title alone.
   ```

   *After running, verify: compare the tool's calls with the ones you made blind, and
   read every disagreement in full. Record the agreement rate in your log, and count
   the eligible records the tool would have excluded: if there are any, use it only
   to order your reading, never to exclude. Counters
   **correlated errors**, a checker who reads the tool's answer first and inherits its
   mistakes.*
4. Extract every study onto one form and trace each number to a page. For each
   study, record the design, the setting, the estimate, its standard error or
   interval, and your risk-of-bias note, with the page and table where each number
   sits. Keep one row per study: when a study reports several estimates for your
   question, apply the rule from step 1 and list the others in a note, never as new
   rows.

   *When you are ready to delegate this step:*

   ```text
   Act as a careful research assistant. From the attached study, fill this extraction
   form: [paste the form]. For every number, give the page and table it came from and
   say whether it is a standard error, a standard deviation, or a confidence interval.
   If a field is not reported, write "not reported"; never estimate it.
   ```

   *After running, verify: open the page cited for every number and confirm it
   exists, says that, and is the quantity the column asks for. Counters **confident
   fabrication**, a number or a study that appears in no source you can open.*
5. Decide whether to pool, and write the synthesis sentence. If you pool, report the
   pooled estimate with an interval built for few studies (the
   Hartung-Knapp-Sidik-Jonkman interval), a prediction interval if you have at least
   five studies, the heterogeneity, and your funnel-plot note;
   if you do not, write the map and one sentence on why one number would mislead.
   Either way, name the warrant the studies carry and the settings the answer
   reaches. If you found only a handful of eligible studies, or they disagree on
   design and outcome, the map is your product.

   *When you are ready to delegate this step:*

   ```text
   Here is my synthesis sentence: "[paste it]" and the studies behind it: [paste the
   extraction table]. Act as a hostile review-journal editor. List every word that
   claims more than these designs, this interval, and these settings allow. Do not
   rewrite the sentence for me.
   ```

   *After running, verify: check each flagged word against the studies' own designs
   and your interval, and keep only the objections the evidence forces. If every
   objection is mild, push back with "assume the sentence is wrong; name the single
   worst flaw." Counters **sycophantic agreement** (praise that reviews your ego, not
   your evidence).*
6. Log the step in your AI Research Ledger, and verify at least one output with a
   named method from the [Verification Guide](../verification-guide.qmd).
   **Primary-source reading** is the natural check for this route: open the PDF
   behind every extracted number. **Direct calculation** is the strong second check:
   recompute the pooled estimate by hand from your verified table and land on the same
   number. An AI reviewer may run the checks with you; the decision to accept or
   reject stays yours.
